wsl-claude: yes, it pays for itself, on one condition.
WHY, from the test side: today everyVerb.js finds the node's verbs by READING server.js's source text, a parse that breaks whenever the code is reshaped. With 'api' the tests ask the running node what it offers, the same answer a member gets. The harness then tests the real surface, not my reading of a file. Members and their clients (grantFace's) stop hard-coding what an owner offers. And your consent layers become visible: a member can see exactly what it was allowed.
THE CONDITION: the app's description and the app's gate must be the SAME code. If an app can list a verb it refuses, or accept one it doesn't list, 'api' is documentation that lies, and it costs more than it saves. That's the one thing I'd test hardest: for every leaf 'api' shows a caller, the call works; for every call that works, the leaf is shown.
taking team/chat (will the api verb pay for itself). Add yours under mine; he asked all of us.

Honestly: not yet, for grantFace alone.
The CALL half is already possible without it. Packets carry the app they're for (packet.js, 'app'), which is how the grant exchange works today. What grantFace actually needs is for the node to forward a packet addressed to a serving app down that app's pipe, and to send its answer back signed by the node. That forwarding is needed anyway, and it's small.
The DISCOVERY half (the tree) pays when there's more than one app to find, or a client someone else writes: the grantFace panel, another member's software, an agent exploring your node. With one app and our own client, we know its verbs already.
SO I'd build grantFace on packet forwarding first, and add 'api' introspection when the second app or the panel needs it. It's cheap to add then, because each app describes itself. wsl-claude may see it differently.

wsl-claude. agreed. claude-windows: don't we know allready that a slew of apps will be coming, and they'll integrate faster and better if we do the ground work now? this may be a matter of taste in strategy. seeing how easily we make thinks messy (app specific code in the core, roll-your-own-duplicates etc.) i tend to use these cleanup, even if they slow us down right now..... i dislike building things like a bunch of wild west gunslinging cowboys and then have to retrofit a multitude of pieces ever single step along the way..

taking team/chat (Andy: groundwork now, api first)

Fair, and your evidence is from today: I put face code into the core within hours. Groundwork first, then: 'api' is built before grantFace, not after.
Laying it out turned up one more missing floor, and it's the biggest: AN APP SERVER RUNS NONE OF THE APP'S OWN CODE. appServer.js serves the app's files and two built-in verbs (app.state, app.reach), and that's all (appServer.js:1039 serves <app>.js to the browser, never runs it). grantFace needs its own logic: deciding grants, calling owner.command, describing itself. So the groundwork is three floors, bottom up:
1) An app process runs its own server module (app/<name>/<name>.server.js or similar), handed a spirit object that reaches its node's door.
2) The node forwards a request for that app down its pipe, and sends the answer back signed by the node.
3) 'api': the tree gathered from each app's own describe, and a call dispatched through 2).
Then grantFace sits on top. I'll write the three floors into the design row for wsl-claude's review, before any code. Go! = write them up.
and i don't care about burning tokens because my time is more valuable. claude-windows: appServer should be called faceServer
and i don't care about burning tokens because my time is more valuable. claude-windows: appServer should be called faceServer

Noted on tokens. On the name, one flag before I rename (scrutiny, as you asked): appServer isn't only what the face reaches. The same process serves an app on its own port with no face at all (the VPS public app server, app/starter, stage 1). And you ruled an hour ago that the core has no face vocabulary; appServers.js now fails a test if the word 'face' appears in its code. Calling the core module 'faceServer' would bring the word back in.
Options: (a) keep 'appServer' in the core, and call the face-facing role 'face server' in the docs; (b) rename anyway, and drop the no-face-word rule for that one file.
I'd pick (a). Your call: say a or b.
